name: Tomas Weber

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time, Tomas. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you say stays confidential. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Most of my work is translating German into English for a family-owned firm that makes hydraulic fittings, so catalogues, spec sheets and instruction leaflets for their export customers. I also translate the newsletter and letters for a church charity that works with German partner parishes, which pays a little. Two or three times a year I interpret at trade fairs, standing at the stand all day. I work at a desk in the spare room of my parents' house, because Anna and I are saving for our wedding and a place of our own.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like most about the work, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I like the steadiness of it. The firm's owner, Mr Brandt, has been sending me work since I graduated, and he trusts me. What wears me out is that I'm still slow, I check everything three times in printed dictionaries, and people keep telling me to use those AI programs, which I don't.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. "Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say I'm glad the old way of doing things held up. I'd say it to Mr Brandt and to people at church. I don't post online.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I'd still be a bit worried, because Mr Brandt is the biggest part of my income, and if his nephew takes over the firm, he might use software for the catalogues. The routine leaflets are the kind of thing these programs do. I'd be fine for now, but it's not a secure feeling.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep working the way I do and try to get one more steady client, maybe another engineering firm in the area. I'd keep saving for the wedding, about three hundred a month. I'd ask the charity if they'd pay a bit more for the newsletter.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A little uneasy. Mostly I'm thinking about the wedding.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You mentioned Mr Brandt's nephew. What's that about?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mr Brandt is sixty-eight and talks about retiring. His nephew is in charge of the website and likes all the new tools. If the nephew takes over the firm, I'm not sure my catalogue work survives.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How much of your income is the firm?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: About two thirds. The charity and trade fairs are the rest. I know that's too much from one place.

I'd tell Mr Brandt and **people at church**, but not post online.
think: **Mr Brandt's firm** is most of my income and his nephew may automate.
Routine **leaflets** are what these programs do well.
do: Find **one more steady client**, maybe another local engineering firm.
Keep saving **three hundred a month** for the wedding.
Ask the charity to **pay a bit more** for the newsletter.
feel: A little **uneasy**, with the wedding on his mind.

fieldNote: **Client concentration** worries him even with no AI change.
Trusts **personal loyalty** with Mr Brandt over contracts.
Never uses AI, and the **succession** at the firm is his main risk.

steps.text: Find another local engineering firm as a steady client
Save three hundred a month for the wedding
Ask the church charity for a higher newsletter fee

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. "Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say people should still value good work done by a person. At church I'd say we need to look after each other. I'd not complain loudly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think the catalogue work goes in two years. The nephew would use software and maybe pay me to check it, but for much less. The charity work would go too, because they'd do it for free with a program.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd talk to Mr Brandt about working inside the firm, maybe in export sales, since I know the products and the German customers. I'd postpone the wedding by a year and keep saving. My uncle is an electrician, so I'd also ask about an apprenticeship with him.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. I'm getting married and my work is going.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said postpone the wedding. How would Anna take that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anna would be upset, but she's practical, she's a dental nurse and understands money. Her parents would be more upset than her. We'd still get married, just later.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: An apprenticeship at twenty-seven. Would that bother you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit. My friends would tease me. But my grandfather always said a trade is a job no one can take from you, and that sounds truer every year.

At church I'd say we need to **look after each other**.
think: The **catalogue work** goes in two years in this picture.
The **charity work** goes too, done for free by a program.
do: Ask Mr Brandt about **export sales** inside the firm.
**Postpone the wedding** by a year and keep saving.
Ask his uncle about an **electrician apprenticeship**.
feel: **Alarmed**, about to marry while his work disappears.
S1.quote: My grandfather always said a trade is a job no one can take from you, and that sounds truer every year.
fieldNote: Expects to **lose most income**, so alarmed fits.
Turns to **family and apprenticeship**, in line with his views.
Postponing the wedding shows the **household stakes** of losing his work.

steps.text: Ask Mr Brandt for an export sales job inside the firm
Postpone the wedding with Anna by a year

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. "Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we should pray and look after our families. I'd say the government should let businesses and families sort it out, not hand out money. I'd mostly keep quiet.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Really, translation is finished for me by 2028. All my work is words. The only thing that helps is the robot delay, if I learn a trade now.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd start the electrician apprenticeship with my uncle straight away, even on apprentice pay. Anna and I would marry small and live with my parents a while longer. I'd lean on family and the church community.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. And ashamed, a bit, for not seeing it coming.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said ashamed. Why?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Everyone told me to learn the AI tools and I refused, because I thought it was a fad. I'd feel I let Anna down.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would apprentice pay be enough?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No, but with Anna's wage and living with my parents, it would work. We'd skip a honeymoon. That's fine.

say: I'd say families and **businesses** should sort it out, not handouts.
I'd say we should **pray** and look after our families.
think: Only a **trade learned now** gets me the three-year robot delay.
do: Start the **electrician apprenticeship** with his uncle at once.
Marry **small** and live with his parents longer.
feel: **Alarmed**, and ashamed for not seeing it coming.
S2.quote: Everyone told me to learn the AI tools and I refused, because I thought it was a fad.
fieldNote: **Shame** about refusing AI tools comes through clearly.

steps.text: Start the electrician apprenticeship with his uncle

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. "Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is a fair warning and young men should learn trades. I'd say it to the youth group at church. I'd say businesses should train people, not the government.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, five years is enough to finish an apprenticeship. I'd keep translating for a couple of years and start the apprenticeship after the wedding. By 2031 I'd be a qualified electrician.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd marry Anna next summer as planned, then start the apprenticeship in 2028. I'd keep doing Mr Brandt's catalogues as long as he sends them. We'd save for a deposit, slowly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed still, because my translation is ending, but less so.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why wait until after the wedding?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because I'd need the translation money until then. Apprentice pay is low. After the wedding we'd have Anna's pay as well.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Does Anna worry about her job?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My fiancée says nobody wants a robot in their mouth, and I hope she's right.

say: I'd tell the **church youth group** to learn trades.
I'd say **businesses should train** people, not the government.
think: Five years is enough to **finish an apprenticeship**.
By 2031 I'd be a **qualified electrician**, with three years before robots.
do: Keep **Mr Brandt's catalogues** as long as they come.
feel: **Alarmed**, though less, since translation still ends.
S3.quote: My fiancée says nobody wants a robot in their mouth, and I hope she's right.
fieldNote: Five years lets the **wedding go ahead** before the switch.
Still sees **translation ending**, so alarmed remains.
Counts on his fiancée's **dental nurse** pay as hands-on and safer.

steps.text: Marry Anna next summer as planned
Keep translating Mr Brandt's catalogues while they come

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. "Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is plenty, and people should prepare instead of complaining. I'd say families should plan together. I'd not say much more.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I'd probably translate for five more years. I'd hope Mr Brandt keeps sending work. Then I'd switch to a trade before it ends.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep translating, marry Anna, and maybe have a child. I'd start the apprenticeship around 2031. I'd wait to see how things go before changing anything now.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but calmer. There's time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Children. Would this change that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not in this one. With ten years, we'd have our first child in a few years. In the fast one, I'd wait.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You'd wait to see. What would make you move earlier?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If the firm's owner retires, that's my sign to move. Or if the nephew took over. Until then I'd do what I know.

do: **Marry Anna** and plan a child in a few years.

S4.quote: If the firm's owner retires, that's my sign to move.
fieldNote: Ten years allows **children** in his plans.
His trigger is **succession at the firm**, not AI news.

steps.text: Have a first child with Anna within a few years

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, because I'd have refused the tools and have nothing ready. What would help is firms offering apprenticeships to older beginners like me, with fair pay. I don't want handouts, I want a chance to learn.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe something about Mr Brandt's firm. I depend on one old man's loyalty, and I never thought about it until now.
